title: The Fisherman and His Wife

full_text:
There was once a fisherman and his wife who lived together in a filthy pigsty of a hovel close by the sea. Every day the fisherman went out with his rod and sat watching the clear water.

One afternoon, his line was pulled deep into the depths. He hauled up an enormous flounder, who spoke in human voice: "Fisherman, spare my life! I am no common fish, but an enchanted prince! Throw me back into the water, I pray you!"

The kind fisherman threw the flounder back: "I would not kill a fish that can speak!"

When he went home and told his wife Ilsebill, she flew into a rage: "Did you ask for nothing in return? It is dreadful to live in this dirty hovel! Go back and ask the fish for a snug little cottage!"

The fisherman went to the sea; the water was green and yellow. He called:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder popped up: "What does she want?"
"She wants a snug cottage."
"Go home; she has it already," said the fish.

The fisherman returned and found a lovely stone cottage with a parlor, garden, and chickens. He was happy, but after a week, Ilsebill grew discontented: "This cottage is too cramped! Go back and tell the flounder I must have a great stone castle with servants and horses!"

The fisherman's heart grew heavy, but he feared his wife. The sea was now dark blue and purple. The fish granted the castle.

Next, Ilsebill demanded to be king: "I must be King of the land!" The sea turned dark gray and foamy; the flounder made her king, with crowns and golden scepters.

Then she demanded: "I must be Emperor!" The sea turned black and stormy; the fish made her Emperor.

Then: "I must be Pope!" The sea heaved with violent breakers, and sky tore with wind; the fish made her Pope, crowned with triple tiaras.

Early the next morning, as the sun began to rise, Ilsebill looked upon the golden dawn from her bed, and shook with rage: "Why can I not command the sun and moon to rise? Go back to the fish! I must become like God Almighty!"

The fisherman trembled in sheer terror. Thunder crashed, lightning cleaved the sky, and mountainous black waves roared like doom. The fisherman shouted against the hurricane:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder surfaced in the storm: "What does she want now?"

"Alas!" wept the fisherman. "She wants to be like God!"

"Go home," spoke the flounder solemnly. "She sits already in her dirty pigsty."

And there they sit to this very day.
moral: Unbridled ambition and insatiable greed eventually strip away everything and return one to the hovel.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Fisherman and His Wife"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.
